comment: THE MODULE OWNS ITS NAME IN ITS OWN FILE. This file is `module-name-collision.toml`, so the module is `module-name-collision`, and it declares a table of exactly that name. Relationships address nodes by NAME, so without a rule every `contains` edge naming it resolves to TWO nodes — the unresolvable-identity class reached through a name collision rather than a missing edge. The module's name is derived from the file's PATH and is not negotiable, so the TABLE takes the suffix. This is the same precedence html uses, where `usedNames` starts `{ [moduleName]: 1 }` so a document node that collides with the file yields rather than the file yielding to a node. The corpus contains two real files of exactly this shape — `doc/book/book.toml` and `doc/contrib/book.toml`, both declaring `[book]` — which is how the rule was found: a hand-written fixture would not have contained it.

expectSymbols.name: module-name-collision
expectSymbols.comment: the file keeps its own name

expectSymbols.name: module-name-collision#2
expectSymbols.comment: the TABLE yields, because the file's identity comes from its path

expectSymbols.name: module-name-collision#2.k
expectSymbols.comment: and the key is prefixed with the ALLOCATED table name, so its edge resolves

forbidSymbols.name: module-name-collision#3
forbidSymbols.comment: nothing beyond the two is allocated — the suffix appears exactly once, because there is exactly one colliding table.

expectRelationships.comment: the source is the module and the target is the TABLE, and the two names differ — which is the whole point: an edge whose source and target share a name cannot say which node it means
